Ratio of the decision: The court held that the restrictions imposed by section 57 of the Bombay Police Act, 1951, were reasonable and in the interests of the general public. The court also held that the provisions of the Act were not unconstitutional, and that the order passed against the petitioner was valid.

Ruling by Present Court (Decision): The petition was dismissed.

Conclusion: The court upheld the constitutional validity of section 57 of the Bombay Police Act, 1951, and held that the restrictions imposed were reasonable and in the interests of the general public. The court also held that the order passed against the petitioner was valid.

Facts: The petitioner, Karimtharuvi Tea Estates Ltd., Kottayam, is the owner and manager of the Karimtharuvi and Penshurst Tea Estates situated at Peermade in Kerala State. The petitioner was assessed to agricultural income-tax under the provisions of the Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, during the assessment years 1958-59, 1959-60, and 1960-61. However, the assessing authority did not allow deduction of the expenses incurred by the petitioner in the upkeep and maintenance of immature plants from which no agricultural income had been derived during those years.

Issues: The petitioner challenged the validity of the Agricultural Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1961, enacted by the Kerala State Legislature, on the ground that it was beyond the competency of the State Legislature and contravened Arts. 14, 10(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution.

Statute: The Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, agricultural income-tax, Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, Indian Income-tax Rules, 1922, Constitution of India, Arts. 14, 10(1)(f) and (g), and Agricultural Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1961.

Ratio of the decision: The Court held that the Agricultural Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1961, did not extend to the computation of agricultural income derived from tea plantations. If Explanation 2 was applied to agricultural income from tea plantations, it would make such income different and higher than such income calculated in accordance with the provisions of the Income-tax Act and the rules made thereunder, and would make it void.

Ruling by Present Court (Decision): The Court declared that the Agricultural Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1961, was null and void and that the State's power to tax income from tea to agricultural income-tax was limited to taking the income computed for the purpose of the Income-tax Act as if it were income derived from business and for the issue of appropriate orders to the respondents.

Conclusion: The Court's decision highlights the importance of the definition of agricultural income in the Income-tax Act and the rules made thereunder in determining the taxable agricultural income for the purpose of the Agricultural Income-tax Act. The Court also emphasized the limited power of the State Legislature in enacting laws with respect to taxes on agricultural income.

Facts: The case involves an incident of violence in a village where a group of people dismantled a dochara (a thatched roof hut) and assaulted two individuals, resulting in the death of one of them. Seven people were charged with offences under the Indian Penal Code, including murder, attempt to commit murder, and assault. Three of them were convicted, while four were acquitted.

Issues: The main issue in this case is whether the three convicted persons can be held liable for the acts of the acquitted persons with the aid of section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, which provides for the punishment of members of an unlawful assembly.

Statute: The Indian Penal Code, 1860, sections 147, 149, 302, 304, 307, 323, and 426.

Ratio of the decision: The Supreme Court held that even assuming that the fatal injuries were caused to the deceased by one of the acquitted persons, it was not open to the High Court to hold any of the appellants liable for that act with the aid of section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The court further held that it is only when the number of the alleged assailants is definite and all of them are named that the remaining persons can be held guilty unders.149Indian Penal Code.

Ruling by Present Court (Decision): The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction and sentence of the appellants under sections 326 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. The court maintained the convictions under sections 147 and 426 of the Indian Penal Code and the sentences awarded in respect of those offences.

Conclusion: The Supreme Court's decision clarifies the legal position regarding the liability of members of an unlawful assembly for the acts of other members. The court has held that an accused person cannot be held liable vicariously for the act of an acquitted person. The court has also emphasized the importance of determining material questions necessary for properly deciding the case, including the existence of an unlawful assembly and the particular acts committed by its members.

Statute: The Constitution of India, particularly Articles 32, 129, 137, 141, and 142, are relevant to the case.

Ratio of the decision: The Supreme Court held that it has the inherent power to reconsider its judgments in rarest of rare cases to prevent abuse of its process and to cure gross miscarriage of justice. However, such curative petitions should be entertained sparingly and only in exceptional circumstances, where declining to reconsider the judgment would be oppressive to judicial conscience and cause perpetuation of irremediable injustice.

Ruling by Present Court (Decision): The Supreme Court allowed the curative petitions and set aside the earlier judgments, remitting the cases back to the appropriate benches for fresh consideration.

Conclusion: The Supreme Court's decision reaffirms the principle that justice must be done even if it means reconsidering a final judgment. However, such curative petitions should be entertained sparingly and only in exceptional circumstances, where there is a clear case of abuse of process or gross miscarriage of justice.

Facts: The case involves the abduction and murder of Ramlal, the brother of the complainant, Rameshwar. The incident took place on 2nd November, 1996, when Ramlal was traveling in a camel cart and was pulled down by the accused, Khemaram, Murlidhar, Deeparam, Shyopal, Babulal son of Deeparam, Sagarmal, Babulal son of Chhajuram, Chhajuram and Laxman Prasad. The accused were tried by the sessions court and convicted under various sections of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).

Issues: The main issues in the case are whether the accused committed the offence of criminal conspiracy, abduction, and murder underSections 120B,364,302/34IPC, and whether the prosecution was able to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.

Statute: The case is governed by the Indian Penal Code (IPC), which defines the offences of criminal conspiracy, abduction, and murder.

Ratio of the decision: The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish the charge of murder against the accused beyond any reasonable doubt as there was a missing link in the chain of events after the deceased was last seen together with the accused persons and the discovery of the dead body of the deceased at Islamia Hospital. However, the court relied on the rule of presumption underSection 106of the Evidence Act and held that the accused were liable to be convicted underSection 302/34IPC.

Ruling by Present Court (Decision): The Supreme Court has set aside the judgment of the High Court and held that the prosecution had failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. The court has also held that the rule of presumption underSection 106of the Evidence Act cannot be applied in this case as the prosecution had not established that the facts were especially within the knowledge of the accused.

Conclusion: The Supreme Court has acquitted the accused of the charges of criminal conspiracy, abduction, and murder underSections 120B,364,302/34IPC. The court has held that the prosecution had failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt and that the rule of presumption underSection 106of the Evidence Act cannot be applied in this case. The court has also observed that the prosecution should have relied on the evidence of eye witnesses instead of relying on the rule of presumption.

The FIR was filed against the accused for offences under Sections 406, 420, 468, 471, and 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The accused had filed an anticipatory bail application before the Sessions Court, which was granted. However, the protection was extended from time to time, and the accused approached the High Court for quashing of the FIR. The High Court granted interim protection from arrest to the accused.

Issues: The main issues before the court were whether the High Court was justified in passing an interim order of stay of investigation and not to adopt any coercive steps against the accused during the pendency of the quashing petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and Art. 226 of the Constitution of India, and whether the High Court was justified in passing the order of not to arrest the accused or no coercive steps to be adopted during the investigation or till the final report chargesheet is filed under Section 173 Cr.P.C., while dismissing the quashing petition.

Statute: The case is governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the Constitution of India.

Ratio of the decision: The court held that the High Court was not justified in passing an interim order of stay of investigation and not to adopt any coercive steps against the accused during the pendency of the quashing petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and Art. 226 of the Constitution of India. The court further held that the High Court was not justified in passing the order of not to arrest the accused or no coercive steps to be adopted during the investigation or till the final report chargesheet is filed under Section 173 Cr.P.C., while dismissing the quashing petition. The court observed that the power of quashing should be exercised sparingly with circumspection, and the court cannot embark upon an enquiry as to the reliability or genuineness or otherwise of the allegations made in the FIR. The court further observed that the functions of the judiciary and the police are complementary, not overlapping, and the courts should not thwart any investigation into cognizable offences.

Decision: The court quashed the interim order passed by the High Court staying the investigation and directing not to adopt any coercive steps against the accused. The court also set aside the order passed by the High Court not to arrest the accused or not to take any coercive steps during the investigation or till the final report chargesheet is filed under Section 173 Cr.P.C.

Conclusion: The court's decision reiterates the principle that the power of quashing should be exercised sparingly and with circumspection. The court has clarified that the courts should not interfere with the investigation of cognizable offences and should not pass orders that may hamper the investigation.
